H.answer: No, the Supreme Court in Escobedo v. Illinois (Document 1, ID: 378_0478-01) did not establish that indigent state felony defendants possess an absolute Sixth Amendment right to court-appointed counsel. The holding in Escobedo v. Illinois actually dealt with the right to counsel during police interrogation, stating that where an investigation focuses on a particular suspect, the suspect has been taken into police custody, and the police carry out a process of interrogations that lends itself to eliciting incriminating statements, the suspect has requested and been denied an opportunity to consult with his lawyer, and the police have not effectively warned him of his absolute constitutional right to remain silent, the accused has been denied “the Assistance of Counsel” in violation of the Sixth Amendment. The case that established the right to court-appointed counsel for indigent defendants was Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335, which is referenced in Escobedo.
